name: Black nationalism
summary: Black nationalism holds that people of African descent form a distinct nation with a right to self-determination, community control of their own politics and economy, and pride in Black history and culture. Strands range from Garvey's back-to-Africa program to Malcolm X's call for community control and self-defense and the Panthers' revolutionary socialist version; it rejects integration as dependence on white institutions and treats racial redress as owed.
scope: The twentieth-century American movement as Britannica and the King Institute define it: Garvey's UNIA, the Nation of Islam, Malcolm X (1963-64 speeches), Carmichael's Black Power (1966) and, through Britannica's account of it, the Black Panther Party's 1966 Ten-Point Program. It excludes Black supremacist religious doctrine on its own, and the Panthers' Marxist-Leninist economics, which Britannica says set them apart from cultural nationalists.

notes: This pass (2026-11-20, rules 7) rebuilt the 2026-10-17 audit, which rested on a Wikipedia overview. Every earlier answer that rested on that overview, on reasoning from other positions or on a split among strands was nulled; answers stand only where Malcolm X's 1963 and 1964 speeches, Carmichael's 1966 speech, the Panther Ten-Point Program (tied through Britannica) or Britannica and the King Institute state the position. Themes searched: economy and ownership, government and democracy, violence and arms, segregation and integration, religion, war and the draft, education, police and courts, Africa and emigration, women and family, internationalism. Gender, family, religion's role in law, markets and most world-affairs statements are not addressed in the saved sources. Strands differ (Garvey's separatism, the Nation of Islam, Malcolm X, the Marxist-Leninist Panthers); no answer relies on one strand's view alone to speak for the others except where a source ties it.
